It is defined as the net movement of particles from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, as a result of their random movement. This process is passive, requiring no external energy input, and is a direct consequence of the intrinsic kinetic energy of particles.

C6.2.title: Chemical Kinetics: Investigating the Factors Affecting the Rate of Reaction

rt.x: Introduction: The Velocity of Chemical Change

The rate of a chemical reaction is a measure of how quickly reactants are converted into products. Some reactions, like the combustion of hydrogen, occur almost instantaneously, while others, like the rusting of iron, take years. Controlling the rate of reaction is vital in industrial chemistry to maximize production while ensuring safety. The IGCSE 0654 Core syllabus requires an identification of the variables that manipulate this rate, an understanding of catalysts, and the ability to interpret experimental data.
1. Factors Influencing the Rate of Reaction
The rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions between particles. Five primary variables can be manipulated to increase this rate:

Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increases the number of particles in a given volume. This leads to more frequent collisions between reactant particles, thereby increasing the reaction rate.

For reactions involving gases, increasing the pressure forces the gas particles closer together (decreasing the volume). This increases the number of particles per unit volume, resulting in more frequent collisions and a faster rate.

Breaking a solid reactant into smaller pieces (or a powder) increases the total surface area exposed to the other reactants. More surface area means more "contact points" for collisions to occur, speeding up the reaction.

Increasing the temperature provides reactant particles with more kinetic energy. Particles move faster and collide more frequently and with more energy. This significantly increases the rate of reaction.
